doc.title: Ronnie Zito interviewed by Monk Rowe & Rick Montalbano, via Zoom, March 9, 2022

title: Woody Herman albums and career mileage; Darin's love of soft playing
summary: Five albums with Woody, Antibes, more mileage than Darin; Darin loved soft sneak-ins.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I’m telling you man it’s amazing. But I’ll tell you man my chops are so strange now from playing the show, I have a lot of bad habits because of the way I’m set up, things like that, and I’ve got some arthritis coming in you know. But I can still play the show, and play pretty strong yet you know. Fast — “Caldonia” is over for me. I did that with Woody for two years and “Northwest Passage” [scats] it was crazy. Woody wanted everything fast. That’s a great band leader. Woody was a great band leader. Great guy man. Boy, miss him. And I did five albums with him. The first album was “My Kind of Broadway.” We did all these Broadway tunes. And he had charts in there from Bill Holman and oh Nat Pierce did a lot, all good music, very good music. And then —
Was it “Live in Antibes” that you did?
Was it, there’s a live thing you did —

Oh yeah, Antibes. Yeah, yeah. That’s right. We didn’t get paid for that for a long time. Yeah we did that and that’s about it, but Woody was a great experience for me. See that’s another thing, when I got off of Woody’s band and I came to New York let’s get that guy that was with Woody. That’s the way it went man. It just does. They hear you, they’re playing a Woody Herman record on the radio locally on the jazz station. Other musicians hear it and — I was getting gigs just because I was with Woody. Actually I got more mileage out of Woody than Bobby Darin. You know? In other words because the musicians were more impressed, and the writers, with somebody from Woody’s band than with Bobby I guess. You know. I don’t know. Although they loved Bobby and some of his stuff was great. He did want to swing all the time. He was right on it man. You know I used to do this thing at the Three Rivers Inn with him, I don’t do it anymore

because I’m not playing that kind of music that much. You know when the drummer sneaks in? You know when you’re playing and you sneak in soft-soft-soft-soft. He never heard that man. He flipped over it. And after a while he’d go, [whispers] “Sneak in, sneak in,” you know while he’s on stage. You know I wouldn’t be playing and he’d go “Sneak in, sneak in, man, sneak in.” And then just soft cymbal, just soft cymbal, and even no hi- hat man. Then all of a sudden a little hi-hat, maybe cross stick you know. He went nuts over that. It was stuff that I heard in the jazz records man, all the stuff we listened to, you know, Blakey and Philly Joe.
